Now let me put together the verse-by-verse notes, drawing from what I have gathered.

---

## 1 Chronicles 14 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

This chapter is a near-duplicate of 2 Samuel 5:11–25. The Chronicler has transposed it, placing it between the unsuccessful and successful attempts to move the ark (1 Chronicles 13 and 15), perhaps to contrast David with Saul, or to show God's blessing on David's reign between two phases of ark-related worship (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-14.html). Ellicott notes that neither Samuel nor the Chronicler observes strict chronological order; the Chronicler may have rearranged material so the ark's removal to Jerusalem follows directly after the city's capture (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/14.htm). Constable sees the chapter as the Chronicler's record of three divine blessings on David: favor with neighbour nations, many children, and victory over the Philistines (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-14.html).

---

### v. 1 — Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, stonemasons, and carpenters, to build a palace for him.

Hiram's embassy is both a political alliance and a mark of David's growing international stature. Guzik (enduringword.com) comments that this shows David's influence and importance: neighbouring kings honoured him with the finest craftsmen and wood. This relationship later continued with Solomon. David and Hiram shared a common enemy in the Philistines — "the enemy of my enemy is my friend" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Precept Austin expands on the cedar: *Cedrus libani* trees could reach 120 feet, were slow-growing (up to 3,000 years), and prized for fragrance, beautiful grain, and high resin content that resisted fungus. By David's time, the legendary cedar forests of Lebanon were already scarce, making the wood exceptionally valuable (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary). 

Matthew Henry notes that even a great king like David needed his neighbours and had reason to be thankful: "David had a very large kingdom, Hiram a very little one; yet David could not build himself a house to his mind unless Hiram furnished him with both workmen and materials" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

The Cambridge Bible observes that the occasion of Hiram's embassy is clearer in 2 Samuel 5:9–11: Hiram heard of David's building works in Jerusalem and sent materials and workmen to assist (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_chronicles/14.htm).

---

### v. 2 — And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had highly exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.

David interpreted Hiram's gesture theologically — as God's confirmation. Ellicott writes: "The willing alliance of the powerful sovereign of Phoenician Tyre was so understood by David. The favour of man is sometimes a sign of the approval of God—always, when it results from well-doing" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/14.htm).

Guzik (enduringword.com) identifies two things David "knew": (1) that the LORD had established him as king — God called and settled him; (2) his kingdom was exalted "for the sake of His people Israel," not for David's personal glory. Every godly leader should know these two things (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Precept Austin adds a third from Guzik: David also knew the kingdom belonged to God — it was *His* kingdom. The commentary quotes John Calvin: "David knew to what end God had exalted his reign: it was because of his people, Israel… It was not for his personal profit but for the common salvation of all." Precept Austin also ties this to the Davidic Covenant (2 Sam 7:16), seeing the ultimate fulfilment in the Messiah's eternal kingdom (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

Mark Boda (cited by Precept Austin) notes: "Israel's royal house functioned as a mediatorial figure serving both as vice-regent of the Lord … and as the one who ensured righteousness, justice, and even blessing for the people of God" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

---

### v. 3 — And David took more wives in Jerusalem and became the father of more sons and daughters.

Every commentator sees this verse as recording a moral failure alongside the outward blessing. Enduring Word calls it "direct disobedience to Deuteronomy 17:17" and notes: "Chronicles makes no mention of David's sin with Bathsheba but after the murder of her husband she was one of the 'more wives' that David added." Guzik adds, "most of the trouble to come in David's life comes from his relationships with women and his children" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Precept Austin draws the same connection to Deuteronomy 17:17 and warns that David "sowed the wind" and Solomon reaped the whirlwind (Hos 8:7). Solomon imitated David's sin, which led to the kingdom's division (1 Ki 11). The page also notes: "Wives in the ancient Near East were a sign of wealth and success and also a way to make political alliance" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) contrasts the wisdom of building a palace with the folly of multiplying wives: "Better far the humble structure with one family dwelling therein in harmony and love, than the imposing mansion wherein dwelt domestic jealousy and strife" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/14.htm).

Matthew Henry observes mildly: "It was David's infirmity that when he settled in his kingdom he took more wives, yet the numerous issue he had added to his honour and strength" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

Constable (evangelical/dispensational) offers an extended discussion on why God blessed David despite his polygamy: Old Testament saints had a different relationship to the Holy Spirit (focused on military enablement rather than character transformation), God's purposes for national Israel differed from those for the church, and the progress of revelation means David's accountability was less than ours (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-14.html).

---

### vv. 4–7 — These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Beeliada, and Eliphelet.

Clarke notes that 2 Samuel 5:14–16 lists only eleven names in the Hebrew text, while the Septuagint has twenty-four; 1 Chronicles lists thirteen, "and all the versions have the same number, with certain varieties in the names" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) remarks that these children, though seen as a sign of blessing, were the seeds of David's worst troubles: "David's after history only too sadly proves that he laid the foundation of his worst troubles when he 'took more wives' to his royal palace and converted what would have been a happy home into an intriguing harem" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/14.htm).

Note on the names: Shammua is also called Shimea; Beeliada ("Baal Knows") is elsewhere called Eliada ("God Knows") — the substitution of "El" for "Baal" may reflect theological editing; Nathan is notable as the ancestor of Jesus (Luke 3:31) as well as Solomon (Matt 1:6). (This information is drawn from multiple standard commentary resources.)

---

### v. 8 — When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went out to face them.

David's consolidation as king of "all Israel" (not just Judah) triggered a full-scale Philistine response. Enduring Word notes a spiritual principle: "David's success brought new challenges from the outside. As God worked mightily in David's life, the devil also got to work and brought opposition against David" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Matthew Henry similarly applies this: "Let the attack which the Philistines made upon David forbid us to be secure in any settlement or advancement, and engage us to expect molestation in this world" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

Clarke references the parallel in 2 Samuel 5:17 and the Targum rendering, which reads "David consulted the WORD of the Lord" for "David inquired of God" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

---

### v. 9 — Now the Philistines had come and raided the Valley of Rephaim.

The Valley of Rephaim lay southwest of Jerusalem and formed part of the boundary between Judah and Benjamin (Josh 15:8). Enduring Word notes it may correspond to the "Valley of Baca" (Ps 84:6), because of the balsam (or mulberry) trees that grew there — literally called "weepers" for their drops of milky sap (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Precept Austin sees the Philistines' aggressive move as a test: the Philistines had dominated Israel during the period of the Judges, Eli, Samuel, and Saul. By detailing these victories, the Chronicler demonstrates God's blessing on David in contrast to Saul's failure (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

---

### v. 10 — So David inquired of God, "Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?" "Go," replied the LORD, "for I will deliver them into your hand."

David's inquiry is a hallmark of his reign. Precept Austin notes: "David's seeking Yahweh shows he is acknowledging that he is dependent on the LORD and is willing to humble himself and seek him instead of relying on his own clever plans." The commentary speculates David may have used the priestly ephod (as in 1 Sam 30:7–8) to inquire (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

Enduring Word: "As David sought God and looked to Him for guidance he was blessed. God honoured David's dependence on Him and gave him the promise of victory" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) draws the application: "This spirit of inquiry and obedience must be ours also. We must not lean on our own understanding, but ask for the guidance of his Spirit" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/14.htm).

Matthew Henry: "Let David's enquiry of God, once and again, upon occasion of the Philistines' invading him, direct us in all our ways to acknowledge God — in distress to fly to him, when we are wronged to appeal to him, and, when we know not what to do, to ask counsel at his oracles" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

---

### v. 11 — So David and his men went up to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, "Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand." So they called that place Baal-perazim.

"Baal-perazim" means "Lord (or Master) of Breakthrough." Guzik notes: "At the battle of Baal Perazim, David defeated the Philistines with an overwhelming force, like a breakthrough of water." Selman (cited by Guzik) observes: "God's 'breakout' in judgment (1 Chron 13:9–12, the death of Uzzah) now becomes a 'breakout' in blessing for Israel" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Ellicott: "True to his character, David owns the mighty hand of God in the results of his own valour… He is conscious of being God's instrument. Contrast the haughty self-confidence of the Assyrian conqueror (Isaiah 10:5–15)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/14.htm).

The Targum (cited by Clarke) renders David's words: "The Lord hath broken the enemies of David like to the breaking of a potter's vessel full of water" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

---

### v. 12 — There the Philistines abandoned their gods, and David ordered that they be burned in the fire.

The Philistines had brought idols into battle — a common ancient Near Eastern practice, expecting their deities to fight for them. David's order to burn them obeyed Deuteronomy 7:5, 25. Enduring Word: "Because David inquired of God and obeyed God, they burned the Philistine idols" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Matthew Henry draws application: "Let David's burning the gods of the Philistines, when they fell into his hands, teach us a holy indignation against idolatry and all the remains of it" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) takes this as a lesson in thoroughness in spiritual warfare: "It is our wisdom to extirpate our enemy; not only to stun but to slay the spiritual foe… Nothing can be more dangerous and unwise than to maintain a dubious and wavering contest with some besetting sin" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/14.htm).

---

### v. 13 — Once again the Philistines raided the valley.

The Philistines return a second time. The repetition sets up a critical contrast: David does not presume on the earlier victory. Enduring Word: "After the first victory over the Philistines, David was wise enough to wait on the LORD before the second battle. It is easy for many in the same situation to say, 'I've fought this battle before. I know how to win. This will be easy'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

---

### v. 14 — So David again inquired of God, who answered him, "Do not march up after them, but circle around them and attack them in front of the balsam trees."

God gives a different strategy for the same enemy. Guzik: "Even against the same enemy, not every battle is the same." Precept Austin notes that the answer here is not a simple "yes" or "no" but specific tactical instructions, suggesting David may have received this by some means other than the ephod — perhaps a dream or prophet (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) observes: "God did not allow David to fight the Philistines when he would have had to engage them at a disadvantage… We are not to expect victory from God if we are negligent of the means we take to win it" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/14.htm).

Constable notes the parallel between Baal-perazim (v. 11, "breaking through" in blessing) and Perez-uzza (1 Chron 13:11, "breaking out" in judgment): "David and the Chronicler emphasized God breaking into the life of His people. In the first instance it was for judgment, but in the second it was for blessing. This record would have encouraged the restoration community" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-14.html).

---

### v. 15 — As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle, because this will mean that God has marched out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.

This is one of the most distinctive verses in the chapter. The "sound of marching" (KJV: "sound of a going") in the treetops was a supernatural signal. Meyer (cited by Guzik): "It was not merely a fitful breeze stealing through the leaves; it was not the going of the wind; but of angel squadrons who were proceeding against the enemies of Israel" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

The Targum (cited by Clarke) interprets: "When thou shalt hear the sound of the angels coming to thy assistance, then go out to battle; for an angel is sent from the presence of God, that he may render thy way prosperous" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

Guzik draws a key application: "When we sense that the LORD is at work, we must go out to battle (advance quickly, 2 Samuel 5:24) and we will see a great victory won." The KJV of 2 Samuel 5:24 says "then thou shalt bestir thyself." Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) emphasized that we must stir ourselves, not merely try to stir others: "Often we think we must stir others up. That often just becomes hype and emotionalism. Instead, stir yourself" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Trapp (cited by Guzik): "We must also, in the spiritual warfare, observe and obey the motions of the Spirit, when he setteth up his standard; for those are the sounds of God's goings, the footsteps of his anointed" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Matthew Henry: "Let the sound of the going in the tops of the mulberry trees direct us to attend God's motions both in his providence and in the influences of his Spirit. When we perceive God to go before us let us gird up our loins, gird on our armour, and follow him" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

Precept Austin notes the species of tree is uncertain: possibilities include pear-tree (LXX), mulberry (AV), aspen (REB, NEB), or balsam (BSB) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

---

### v. 16 — So David did as God had commanded him, and they struck down the army of the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer.

David's obedience is total and the victory is sweeping. Guzik: "He did this by waiting for evidence of God's work and then giving himself completely to the battle" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

Payne (cited by Guzik): "Because he looked to the Lord for his strength and for his strategy, he was able to beat back the Philistine offences, to secure the independence of God's people, and to terminate forever the threat of Philistine conquest and oppression" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

---

### v. 17 — And David's fame went out into every land, and the LORD caused all nations to fear him.

This verse is unique to Chronicles — it does not appear in the 2 Samuel parallel. Ellicott notes: "It looks like a concluding reflection of the chronicler's, similar to 2 Chronicles 17:10; 2 Chronicles 20:29. Yet this fear was, as we should say, the natural effect of his victories. In the view of the chronicler, David's success in arms, with all its consequences, was the work of Jehovah" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/14.htm).

Clarke adds the qualification: "all lands" means "all the surrounding or neighbouring lands and nations, for no others can possibly be intended" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

Matthew Henry sees a typological dimension: "Let the reputation which David obtained … be looked upon as a type and figure of the exalted honour of the Son of David… Thus has God highly exalted our Redeemer, and given him a name above every name" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

Precept Austin notes that this verse forms a bookend with v. 2, framing the whole chapter with statements of God's blessing on David among the nations (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

---

### Denominational Distinctives

**On David's polygamy (v. 3):**

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik): Calls it "direct disobedience to Deuteronomy 17:17" and a "moral failure" that "sowed seeds of trouble to come." Notes that David handled trials better than success (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/).

- **Reformed** (John Calvin, cited at Precept Austin): Calvin does not directly comment on the polygamy in this passage (the citation focuses on v. 2), but the Reformed tradition generally views David's multiple wives as sin, not merely cultural practice (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

- **Evangelical/Dispensational** (Constable): Gives the most extended defence of why God blessed David despite polygamy: the Holy Spirit's ministry in the OT focused on military enablement, not character transformation; God's purposes in national Israel differed from the church; and the progress of revelation means David had less accountability. "God was more merciful with David's polygamy in view of His purposes then. In view of His purposes now, He requires a higher degree of personal holiness" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-14.html).

- **Methodist/Wesleyan** (Clarke): Clarke simply notes the parallel with 2 Samuel 5 without moral comment on polygamy, though his notes on the parallel passage may differ (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

- **Puritan/Classic Evangelical** (Matthew Henry): Calls it David's "infirmity," taking a gentler line: "It was David's infirmity that when he settled in his kingdom he took more wives, yet the numerous issue he had added to his honour and strength" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-14.html).

**On the "sound of marching" (v. 15) and supernatural guidance:**

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Guzik / Enduring Word): Emphasises that God still provides supernatural guidance. Quotes Adam Clarke's pointed question: "How is it that such supernatural directions and assistances are not communicated now? Because they are not asked for; and they are not asked for because they are not expected; and they are not expected because men have not faith" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-14/). Also emphasises sensing the Spirit's movement and "bestirring thyself" (a Spurgeon theme).

- **Reformed** (Calvin, cited in Precept Austin): Calvin's emphasis on this chapter falls on v. 2 — the purpose of exaltation being for God's people, not self — rather than on the mode of guidance (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).

---

### Other Views

**Targum (Jewish interpretive tradition):** Adam Clarke's commentary preserves several Targum readings, marked "- T." The Targum consistently replaces "God" or "the LORD" with "the WORD of the Lord" (v. 10: "David consulted the WORD of the Lord"; v. 15: "an angel is sent from the presence of God"), reflecting an intertestamental Jewish tendency to avoid direct anthropomorphism (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-14.html).

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to locate specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentary on this chapter within the search limits. Haydock's Catholic Commentary is listed as available at StudyLight.org for 1 Chronicles 14 but was not fetched.

**Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible notes that the Chronicler derives this chapter from Samuel but places it differently. 2 Samuel has the two Philistine battles immediately before the ark's removal; the Chronicler inserts them between the first (failed) and second (successful) ark attempts, for theological rather than chronological reasons (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_chronicles/14.htm). Precept Austin cites Frederick Mabie, who explains: the chapter is out of chronological order, "perhaps as a means of contrasting the house of David and the house of Saul" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary). The NET Bible notes were not accessed due to search limits.

**On the tree species (v. 14–15):** The Hebrew *beka'im* is uncertain. As noted by Precept Austin and Selman: possibilities include balsam (BSB), mulberry (KJV, AV), pear-tree (LXX), or aspen (REB, NEB). No consensus exists among scholars (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-14-commentary).
